Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Cameroon predominantly use paper-based registers and manual forms for patient data recording at point-of-service. Individual client data management functions adequately in only 26% of facilities (urban study), with clinical staff handling data alongside duties using physical tools; electronic patient files are proposed but not implemented routinely. Aggregated data for DHIS2 reporting is compiled manually and entered at district level, not digitally at clinics. Pilots exist for EMRs like OpenMRS/GNU Health in specific regions (e.g., East/Centre for HIV/TB) and DAMA electronic registers in 154 PEPFAR sites, but these are isolated, program-specific, and not representative of most rural clinics. National DHIS2 is scaled but for aggregate reporting, not point-of-care patient records. Key barriers include poor electricity/internet in rural areas (avg. 6.9km to power; low 3G/4G), low computer access (32% facilities), lack of ICT skills among staff, high poverty, and governance gaps (85% unaware of digital health policies). National Digital Health Strategy 2020-2024 aims for EMR in 70% facilities by 2024, but rural reality lags far behind urban/national ambitions, with paper default and digital limited to upward reporting/pilots.

revision_notes: Original score of 1 (Entirely paper) reflected the dominant reality but understated genuine, functioning (if isolated) digital data-capture programmes operating in specific rural facilities: DAMA electronic registers used at 154 PEPFAR-supported sites, OpenMRS/GNU Health EMR pilots in East/Centre regions for HIV/TB, and the BornFyne prenatal digital platform operating across four health districts including rural settings. A 2025 nationwide survey (data collected Jan-Apr 2024, n=60 organisations) found only 32.1% of health facilities have their own computers and 27% have internet access, confirming paper remains dominant, but these named, operational (not merely planned) digital tools mean 'entirely paper' undersells actual facility-level practice. Recalculated to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital).
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Cameroon remain predominantly paper-based for point-of-service data capture, with only around 32% of health facilities possessing their own computers and 27% having internet access as of 2024. However, some rural and semi-rural facilities do use functioning digital tools alongside paper registers: DAMA electronic registers operate across 154 PEPFAR-supported HIV/TB sites, OpenMRS/GNU Health electronic medical record pilots run in the East and Centre regions, and the BornFyne prenatal digital platform has been deployed across four health districts with rural coverage. National DHIS2 remains an aggregate reporting tool fed by manually compiled data rather than a point-of-care system. The National Digital Health Strategic Plan 2020-2024 targets electronic medical records in 70% of facilities, a goal not yet met in rural areas given persistent barriers of unreliable electricity and internet, low digital literacy among staff, and underinvestment in ICT infrastructure.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Cameroon, primarily Gendarmerie Nationale brigades/posts (444 brigades, 160 posts), record case files, complaints, and incident reports using handwritten procès-verbaux (PVs) and paper files, as standard in francophone Africa and per Criminal Procedure Code. Criminal records derived from these are manually stored in hardcopy at courts/Ministry of Justice; police do not maintain digital criminal records. No evidence of digital case management systems, rural pilots, or IT for incident reporting found on official sites, despite general digital pushes (e.g., civil registration). Paper-based at facility level; any later court entry does not qualify as digital at rural station per rules. Gendarmerie, Records Paper, CPC

A 2025 legal analysis of Cameroon's civil and criminal records management (IJNRD, April 2025) explicitly describes the current regime as paper-based nationally, with no evidence of a digital case management system in use, and recommends transition to an electronic approach. revised_comments: Rural police stations in Cameroon, overwhelmingly gendarmerie brigades and posts (444 brigades and 160 posts nationwide), record case files, complaints and incident reports by hand using paper procès-verbaux, as required under the 2005 Criminal Procedure Code. A 2025 academic review of Cameroon's civil and criminal records management confirms the country continues to operate a paper-based regime nationally, citing high management costs, risk of physical loss or damage, and slow retrieval, while calling for an electronic-based approach going forward. No digital case management system, incident database, or IT-based record-keeping has been identified in rural police facilities; any subsequent digitisation occurs later at courts or the Ministry of Justice, outside the scope of facility-level data capture.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices (2,350 secondary civil status centers in villages) predominantly use paper-based recording for births and other vital events, as the national system was not computerized as of 2018-2019 reports.UNECA CRVS Snapshot New 2024 law (Law No. 2024/016) introduces digital certificates, UPIN, national database, and pilot phases for computerization, with first digital births issued in select urban councils in 2026 (e.g., Limbe I).Journal of Digital Technologies and Law; UNDP Strategic plan (2025-2029) aims for full digital by 2029, but current rollout limited to pilots/donor projects in handful of municipalities, not majority rural facilities.Vital Strategies Key barriers: poor infrastructure/internet in rural areas, low digital literacy, distance/cost to centers, backlog under-registration.UNECA CRVS Snapshot; Journal of Digital Technologies and Law National ambition for digital CRVS contrasts with rural paper reality; no evidence of predominant point-of-service digital use in rural registries.

revision_notes: Original score of 1 (Entirely paper) understated an active, several-year-old digitalisation programme already reaching some rural registry offices, not merely an isolated 2026 urban pilot as the original comment characterised it. A UNDP/BUNEC 'Legal Identity and Social Cohesion' project, running since 2020 (Japan-funded phase) and expanded 2024-2025 (Denmark-funded phase), has equipped 26 civil status centres around Maroua (Far North) with computers, biometric kits and dedicated software producing over 50,000 digital civil status documents, and is expanding to ten further centres including rural Far North localities (Koza, Meri, Mindif, Mora). Rural secondary centres such as Dougoui process around 7 digital registrations weekly. This is genuine, operating (not merely piloted or planned) digital data capture in a meaningful number of rural registry offices, alongside the great majority nationally (c. 2,350 secondary centres) still on paper. Recalculated to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) rather than confirming 1; not raised further as this remains a minority of total rural registry offices nationally.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Cameroon are overwhelmingly paper-based, but a genuine and growing digital footprint now exists at facility level in some rural areas. Since 2020, a UNDP-BUNEC partnership funded first by Japan and, from 2024-2025, by Denmark, has equipped civil status centres in the Far North region (including rural localities such as Gazawa, Kaele, Mokolo, Tokombéré, Touloum, Koza, Meri, Mindif and Mora) with computers, biometric kits, printers and dedicated software, enabling over 50,000 digital civil status documents to be issued across 26 centres, with rural secondary centres such as Dougoui processing several digital registrations each week. Law No. 2024/016, enacted in December 2024, establishes a legal basis for a Unique Personal Identification Number and digital civil status certificates with the same legal value as paper documents, though nationwide activation of digital certificate issuance depends on further presidential decrees and full rollout is targeted for 2029. Outside these donor-supported centres, the great majority of Cameroon's roughly 2,350 secondary civil status centres continue to rely on manual, paper-based registration, with poor rural connectivity, low digital literacy, and distance to registration centres remaining significant barriers.

revision_notes: Confirmed. A 2023 Global Partnership for Education Independent Technical Advisory Panel (ITAP) review of Cameroon's education data systems explicitly notes 'a heavy dependence on paper collection rather than digitalisation' at school level, and that EMIS platforms (SIGE) operate at a higher aggregation level, not point-of-service. Score of 1 (Entirely paper) confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Cameroon rely almost entirely on paper-based registers for recording attendance, administrative data and learning outcomes at point of service. Only around 3% of public primary schools possess computers, and where ICT is taught it is overwhelmingly theoretical owing to a lack of equipment. National Education Management Information System platforms (SIGE/STATEDUC), overseen separately by each of Cameroon's education ministries, aggregate statistics at central and regional level from paper-based school returns rather than capturing data digitally at the facility. A 2023 independent review for the Global Partnership for Education confirms continued heavy reliance on paper collection rather than digitalisation across the sector's data systems. Isolated digital pilots exist (for example UNICEF's 'Connect My School' e-container initiative) but remain limited to single sites rather than representative of the rural school network as a whole, which continues to face shortages of electricity, internet connectivity, computer equipment and teacher ICT training.
